newsitem.title: NORWAY: Arafat to Oslo to review deadlocked peace process.
newsitem.headline: Arafat to Oslo to review deadlocked peace process.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat travels to Oslo on Monday to review the deadlocked Middle East peace process which started with secret talks under Norwegian mediation three years ago.
In Israel, U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross said Arafat's European trip would hamper mediation efforts.

Arafat's official two-day visit, his first to Norway since becoming president in January, takes place at the invitation of the Norwegian government, which helped broker the 1993 Israeli-Palestinian pact on Palestinian self-rule.

The Palestinian leader will be the first foreign dignitary to be welcomed by the new Norwegian Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland, who succeeded political veteran and fellow Labour Party member Gro Harlem Brundtland on Friday.
Arafat will hold talks with Jagland and Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal, who extended the invitation to Arafat during a visit to the Middle East earlier this month.
"There will be a full review of the peace process," a foreign ministry spokesman said, but he added that no talks with Israeli officials were planned.

Ross, trying to seal an Israeli-PLO deal on the volatile West Bank town of Hebron, met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday and Israel Radio said he would travel to the Gaza Strip for talks with Arafat.
"It's clear that we have further narrowed the differences that exist but we have not overcome those differences," Ross told reporters after meeting Netanyahu in northern Israel.

"Clearly the pace of negotiations is affected when the leaders are not here. Also my own presence is affected when the leaders aren't here because part of my mission is very clearly to go back and forth between the leaders," Ross said.

Israel's former Labour government agreed more than a year ago to redeploy troops away from Hebron, home to 100,000 Palestinians and 400 Jewish settlers, but delayed the pullout after suicide bombings by Moslem militants killed 59 people in the Jewish state in February and March.
In Oslo, Arafat will rendezvous with his friend Terje Roed Larsen, who until Friday was special U.N. coordinator for Gaza and Norway's trouble-shooter in the Middle East.
Larsen, one of the Norwegian diplomats who helped broker the Israeli-Palestinian pact, is moving back home from the turbulent Middle East to head a portfolio for national planning.

"I am afraid the Middle East will move from crisis to crisis for many years to come and I felt I had now reached a point where it was natural for me to take on other tasks," he told reporters after taking office on Friday.

Some commentators said it was unwise to bring home Larsen at a time when he had sought to help pull the peace process back on track. But others said Oslo no longer played the role it did when it supervised the peace talks.
However, Norway keeps observers in Hebron and chairs an ad hoc liaison committe of donor countries to Palestinians.
Arafat shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize with then-Israeli Foreign Minister Shimon Peres and late Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin for the now-troubled agreement on Palestinian self-rule.

On Tuesday, Arafat will be received in audience by King Harald V before holding final talks with Godal and leaving for Dublin, where the Palestinian leader will meet Ireland's prime minister, foreign minister and president during a two-day visit.
Ireland now holds the rotating European Union presidency and its foreign minister, Dick Spring, went to Israel and Gaza earlier this month to lend EU support to the peace process.
